analysis.one_liner: Blocks states from punishing anyone who travels out of state for legal reproductive health care.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 35 Senate sponsors in June 2026 and sent to the Judiciary Committee, the bill has seen no further action in a Congress that runs to January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it unlawful for any person or government to restrict, punish, or discriminate against someone who travels to another state to get or provide reproductive health care that is legal there, including someone who helps arrange the trip [S2][S3]. It also protects doctors and clinics in states where the care is legal from being penalized for treating out-of-state patients [S3]. To enforce this, it lets the Justice Department sue states and officials, gives individuals and providers their own right to sue, waives state and official immunity, preempts conflicting state laws, and lets defendants move state-court cases into federal court [S3]. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and has seen no further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Women in states that ban or restrict abortion who need to travel for care, along with the doctors, clinics, family members, and organizations that help them travel and pay for it. The bill would give them federal protection against state investigation, penalties, and lawsuits tied to legal out-of-state care [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for any person or government to restrict, sanction, or discriminate against someone who travels to another state for legal reproductive health care, or who helps someone make that trip.
It shields doctors and clinics in states where the care is legal from being penalized for treating out-of-state patients, including staff and patients who might be affected.

It gives affected individuals and providers their own right to sue, lets the Justice Department sue states and officials, waives governmental immunities, and lets defendants move state-court prosecutions or suits that interfere with travel into federal court.
It preempts state laws that conflict with it, so state-level travel restrictions or retaliation would have no legal effect.

analysis.who_pays: States and local officials that restrict or punish out-of-state reproductive care would face lawsuits and federal preemption of those laws; anti-abortion organizations and private parties who bring legal action against travelers or their helpers could be sued and would bear litigation costs [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill waives state sovereign and official immunity and preempts any inconsistent state law, which courts hostile to the measure could find exceeds Congress's enforcement power under the Fourteenth Amendment, so parts of it might not survive a legal challenge.

It creates litigation exposure for state and local officials enforcing anti-abortion laws, and gives prevailing plaintiffs court-awarded attorney's fees, which critics would call an unbalanced enforcement design.
It does not itself fund or provide reproductive care; women in ban states must still travel, pay for care, and enforce their own rights in court, so the practical burden of state bans remains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers meaningful, low-cost legal protection to women in ban states and to the doctors and helpers who serve them, and it does not spend public money; its drawbacks are legal (it leans on contested readings of the Fourteenth Amendment's enforcement power, and immunity waivers may not survive court review) and political (it preempts state laws and will face unified opposition from one party). The main honest objection is that it may overreach federal power over state criminal and family law; the honest cost is that it does nothing to restore care in states where abortion is banned and no one travels.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2026, and nothing has happened to it since — it has not been voted on and, as a Democratic bill with no Republican cosponsors in this Senate, is unlikely to advance.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on June 8, 2026 and read twice before being referred to the Judiciary Committee.
Thirty-five senators — 34 Democrats and 1 independent — signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans did.
The action record shows no committee vote, no floor action, and no vote of any kind since the referral.
The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically still alive but has sat untouched in committee since its introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Anti-abortion state officials and organizations that rely on state law to restrict travel for care are better off that the bill has gone nowhere. Women in abortion-ban states, who would have gained federal protection against those penalties, are worse off.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 35 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 35 Senate Democrats and independents (including Sanders, Warren, Murray, Klobuchar, Booker)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors are Democrats or independents, with no Republican support in the Senate, where the Republican party holds a majority.

industries.industry: Abortion and reproductive health care providers
industries.note: The bill protects out-of-state providers from being sanctioned or sued for treating patients from ban states, and lets providers sue on behalf of their staff and patients. It expands their legal footing but does not route public money through them.

industries.industry: Anti-abortion organizations and enforcement-oriented state officials
industries.note: Groups and officials that use state law to punish travel for abortion or to pursue out-of-state providers would lose their main enforcement tools, since the bill preempts inconsistent state laws and waives state immunity from suit.

analysis.trajectory: With 35 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, in a Senate controlled by Republicans, the bill has essentially no path: it will most likely remain in the Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote and die when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, as similar bills have.
